newsitem.title: THAILAND: Fighting flares in last Cambodian opposition town.
newsitem.headline: Fighting flares in last Cambodian opposition town.

text.p: Gun and mortar fire rocked the last town held by loyalists of ousted co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Tuesday as Cambodian government forces fought to seize control of it, military officials said.

"There was a heavy exchange of gunfire this morning and dozens of mortar shells have already been fired by the defensive (royalist) faction," a Thai military official said of the town of O'Smach, just over the border in Cambodia.
General Chea Sarorn, a commander of government forces, told Reuters in Phnom Penh the government side had pushed into the area around the O'Smach market.
"The government soldiers are in O'Smach next to the market and fighting is going on," he said, adding that the government hoped to seize the town on Tuesday.
Hours earlier more than 20,000 civilians fled O'Smach into Thailand to escape the fighting.

Thai authorities said they opened gates at a checkpoint and allowed the civilians to walk across the border to Kab Choeng district late on Monday after government troops captured the strategic hill of Khao Laem five km (three miles) from O'Smach.
The refugees spent the morning at a border market two km (one mile) inside Thailand and later moved on foot to Huay Choeng, six km (four miles) from the border.
The lines of fleeing Cambodians stretched along the entire six km from the market to Huay Choeng, witnesses said.
The Thai army had sent reinforcements into the area and sealed off the border in anticipation of Tuesday's fighting.
About 2,000 civilians remain in O'Smach, where they plan to wait out the fighting, witnesses said.
"We can live under the control of any faction. We are merchants, not politicians," one trader from O'Smach told Reuters.

Fighting between government forces under the control of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen and ousted First Prime Minister Ranariddh's ragged army has continued sporadically since Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh on July 6.

The prince's forces were pushed into Cambodia's northwest, where they are making their last stand around the border town of O'Smach with assistance from at least 1,000 Khmer Rouge rebels, royalist troops said.
On Tuesday, heavily armed Khmer Rouge were seen moving into positions in O'Smach to bolster the royalist opposition forces.
Major Yen Bunsrun of Ranariddh's army said he was getting support from about 1,000 Khmer Rouge, Maoists who ruled Cambodia during the 1975-79 "Killing Fields" years.
"We will not let the puppet troops of Hun Sen capture our last stronghold. Wait and see our response," he said over a barbed wire fence at the border as mortar fire echoed behind him.
"Even if they capture the town, Hun Sen's troops will not be able to hold it for more than three days," he said.
Hun Sen has justified his power grab by accusing Ranariddh of smuggling weapons and bringing Khmer Rouge into the capital Phnom Penh.
On Monday he said Ranariddh would have to face those charges in court on his return to Cambodia, as well as answer for fighting alongside Khmer Rouge in the northwest.
